extracted.intended_audience: Patent office classifiers, patent examiners, patent searchers, and other professional users of the IPC (WIPO)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and mandatory rules for classifying patent documents using the International Patent Classification (IPC) core and advanced levels, including symbol layout, hierarchy, selection rules, references, indexing, and search use. Intended to direct how to place invention information in the IPC and how to use the IPC for searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections as highest hierarchical level
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is divided into eight sections (A–H). Sections are the highest level of hierarchy and each section title is a very broad indication of content. Subsections (informative headings) may be used within sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section symbol is one capital letter (A–H). Section titles are followed by a summary of main subdivisions. Use sections as the top-level partition when locating subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class symbol and title format
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section is subdivided into classes (second hierarchical level). A class symbol consists of the section letter followed by a two-digit number (e.g., H01). The class title gives an indication of the content; some classes have an index summarising content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read class titles as broad indicators only; consult subclass and group levels for precise placement. Use class indexes where provided for quick orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subclass symbols, titles and guidance headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Each class comprises one or more subclasses (third hierarchical level). A subclass symbol consists of the class symbol followed by a capital letter (e.g., H01S). Subclass titles indicate the content as precisely as possible. Where a large part of a subclass relates to common subject matter a guidance heading may be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subclass indices provide an informative survey. Electronic IPC allows viewing subclass content by complexity. Guidance headings mark common subject matter at the start of parts of a subclass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group symbols: main groups and subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: Each subclass is broken into groups which are either main groups (fourth level) or subgroups (lower levels). A group symbol is the subclass symbol followed by numbers separated by an oblique stroke. Main group symbols end with '/00'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main group titles precisely define a field useful for search purposes and are printed in bold. Subgroup numbering after the slash is a decimal subdivision of the preceding digit; dots used in presentation indicate hierarchical indentation and dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete classification symbol composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete classification symbol comprises the combined symbols representing the section, class, subclass and main group or subgroup (e.g., H01S 3/00).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning or citing a place, use the full combined symbol that identifies section→class→subclass→group (and subgroup) to precisely indicate the place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of hierarchy (indentation/dots determine hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC is hierarchical: section → class → subclass → group → subgroup. The hierarchy among subgroups is determined solely by the number of dots (indentation) preceding their titles, not by numbering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret subgroup titles as restricted by the titles of groups under which they are indented. Use indentation/dots to determine parent/child relations (examples provided in guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-level IPC: core level (mandatory minimum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC has two levels: core and advanced. Industrial Property Offices are required to classify published patent documents at least according to the core level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core level is intended for general information and searching smaller collections; it includes hierarchically high entries (sections, classes, subclasses, main groups and some subgroups). Printed IPC includes only the core level. Core-level revisions are included only with a new edition (three-year revision cycles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-level IPC: advanced level (optional, continuous revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The advanced level is intended for searching larger, international collections and is not mandatory. It contains more detailed subdivisions compatible with the core level and is revised continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices may adopt advanced-level entries if desired; advanced-level amendments are prepared through an accelerated continuous procedure and may later be incorporated into a new core-level edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of main groups within a subclass
rubrics_metrics.description: Main groups in each subclass are arranged in a sequence intended to assist the user, generally from the most complex or highly specialised subject matter to the least. A residual main group (e.g., 'not otherwise provided for') is placed at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading a subclass, expect specialised/complex main groups first. The residual group is last and should be used only for subject matter not covered elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance headings to indicate common subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When several successive main groups relate to common subject matter, a short underlined 'guidance heading' before the first group indicates that common subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guidance heading's scope extends to the next guidance heading or a heavy rule line. In exceptional cases, a guidance heading may cover a single main group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of titles (multipart titles and interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles may use single or several related phrases linked together; multipart titles separated by semicolons should be interpreted as separate titles, each part treated independently when convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A multipart title is used to group distinct kinds of subject matter. When a title is a continuation of a higher-level title, capitalization and punctuation indicate dependence; always read subgroup titles as dependent upon their parent titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: functions (limiting, precedence, guidance/informative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference (phrase in brackets referring to another place) shows that subject matter indicated by the reference is covered by the place referred to. References have functions: (a) Limitation of scope (limiting reference) — excludes specified subject matter and indicates where it is classified; (b) Indication of precedence — states that another place 'takes precedence' so subject matter classifiable in more than one place should be classified only in one; (c) Guidance — informative references indicate related subject matter of interest for searching but not within the scope of the place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting and precedence references are critical for correct classification and are included both in schemes and the electronic layer. Informative references are progressively moved to the electronic layer to keep printed schemes readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and interpretation of references (placement, scope, reading rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is usually placed at the end of the title to which it belongs. A reference following a class/subclass/group title relates to all hierarchically inferior places; a reference in a guidance heading or note relates to all groups covered by that heading or note. In printed schemes, references within a subclass quote only the number of the referred group (not the subclass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple items are referred to the same place, separate them by commas with the symbol given at the end. References to different places are separated by semicolons. Be mindful that a quoted group is usually the most relevant but not necessarily the only relevant group—hierarchically related groups should also be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes: defining/explaining scope (override general guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes define or explain specific words, phrases or the scope of places, or indicate how subject matter is classified. Notes may be associated with section, subclass, guidance heading or group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes apply only to the places concerned and override any general guidance in case of conflict. Use notes to resolve ambiguities and classification exceptions (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of places: what constitutes subclass/main group/subgroup coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of subclasses, main groups and subgroups define the intended content; subgroup titles must be read as dependent upon and restricted by the titles of the groups under which they are indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgroup titles that begin with a lowercase letter are continuations of the higher-level title; capitalized subgroup titles are complete expressions but are restricted by hierarchical position. Always interpret a subgroup within the context of its parent titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should represent invention information primarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention information comprises all novel and unobvious subject matter in a patent document's total disclosure and is the primary matter to be represented by classification (usually determined using the claims for guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify invention information first. 'Inventive thing' and 'invention information' are the core focus—classification should aim to represent these novel aspects completely; additional (non-inventive) information may be classified as secondary if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish invention information from additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional information may be technical matter present in the document that supplements invention information (e.g., background, preferred embodiments) and may be classifiable but is not the core invention information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning multiple classifications, prioritize invention information. Additional information can justify secondary classification or indexing but should not obscure the primary inventive subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of technical subject matter categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC recognises categories of subject matter (methods of using a product/non-manufacturing processes; products/articles of manufacture; processes of making a product; apparatus; materials). Classification places are provided for chemical compounds, chemical mixtures/compositions, preparations/treatments, apparatus/processes, articles of manufacture, multistep processes/industrial plants, details/constructional parts, general chemical formulae and combinatorial libraries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the classification place based on the technical category relevant to the invention (e.g., for compositions choose composition place unless the process is the novel aspect). Use the glossary and notes for category-specific nuances (examples and exceptions given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-aspect (multiple) classification of technical subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different aspects of a technical subject are classifiable in different places, multiple classification should be applied so that all relevant aspects are represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For searching, combine classification symbols or symbols plus indexing codes to narrow queries. Apply multiple classifications when invention information spans aspects (e.g., device + process + material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schemes for secondary classification, hybrid systems and indexing codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary classification schemes, hybrid systems and indexing schemes (indexing codes) may be used to provide additional, non-hierarchical search access or to represent subject matter not adequately captured by the places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid and indexing systems complement hierarchical classification: use them to improve retrieval. Informative references are often migrated to the electronic layer; indexing codes can be used to augment or refine search queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligatory vs non-obligatory classification and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Obligatory classification is the classification necessary to completely represent the invention information of a patent document. Non-obligatory classification and non-obligatory indexing provide supplementary subject-matter representation at the discretion of the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices must ensure obligatory classification covers invention information. Non-obligatory classification/indexing may be used for additional searchability or to represent secondary aspects; procedures differ by publication level and office practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification procedure for different publication levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Different procedures apply depending on publication level: patents granted after search and examination, searched but unexamined patent applications, and unsearched patent documents have distinct recommended classification treatments and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify patents granted after search/examination according to the most complete available information; for searched but unexamined documents apply search-determined classifications; for unsearched documents apply general classification guidance and be aware of potential later reclassification after examination or revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for selecting a subclass
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for selecting a subclass includes choosing the subclass whose title and scope best cover the invention information while considering references, notes and the hierarchical structure. (See paragraphs 136–138.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with broad subclass titles and narrow down to groups/subgroups; respect limiting references and precedence that may exclude apparent coverage; when in doubt consult notes, references, and electronic layer definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for selecting a group (main group/subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the group whose title and definition most precisely define the invention information; subgroup titles must be read as dependent on parent group titles. (See paragraphs 139–140.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer groups that explicitly define the essential features of the invention. Use the standardised ordering (complex → simple) and residual groups only when no other place applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common rule for classification and reading group titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Group titles, subgroup titles and their indentation indicate limits and dependencies; a subgroup title is often a continuation of the parent and must be read in context. (See paragraphs 141–145.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret titles syntactically and hierarchically: lowercase subgroup entries are continuations; capitalized subgroup entries are complete expressions but limited by indentation. Do not ignore indentation context when assigning classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority rules: First-place priority and Last-place priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority rules resolve where to classify subject matter classifiable in more than one place: First-place priority assigns subject matter to the first place indicated by rules; Last-place priority assigns it to the last place in a series depending on specific guidance. (See paragraphs 146–154.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the First Place Priority Rule where appropriate (assign to the principal place). Use Last Place Priority for series-dependent situations as described in the Guide. Follow specific examples and precedence references in the scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classification situations are subject to special rules described in the Guide that override general selection and priority rules. (See paragraph 155.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult special rules where explicitly indicated in a subclass or group; special rules may address exceptional treatment of particular subject matter or procedural situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of classification symbols and indexing codes on patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guide specifies how IPC symbols and indexing codes should be presented on patent documents, including the indication of the IPC edition (e.g., Int.Cl. (2006)). (See paragraphs 156–161.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow formatting rules for symbol order and edition indication. The abbreviation 'Int.Cl.' may precede classification symbols; the year of the edition is shown in round brackets after 'Int.Cl.' for 2006 and later editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special classification places for subject matter not adequately covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Where subject matter is not adequately covered elsewhere in the IPC, special places may be provided to accommodate that subject matter. (See paragraphs 162–165.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these special places when no normal place applies; consult the Guide’s examples and the electronic layer for supplementary information and appropriate special-place selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the IPC for search purposes (defining a field of search)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on searching includes different kinds of search, preparing for a search, defining the field of search and recommended combinations of classification symbols and indexing codes for specificity. (See paragraphs 166–178.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex subjects, start with combinations of classification symbols and indexing codes to narrow searches; broaden queries afterward if needed. Failure to retrieve relevant documents may indicate incorrect choice of IPC place—reconsider wording and redefine the field of search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master Classification Database (MCD) usage and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The MCD is a bibliographic database storing bibliographic elements (including IPC symbols) of patent documents at their publication levels; it stores documents classified according to the current core level and the continuously updated advanced level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MCD copies or online access to retrieve classification and bibliographic data. The MCD facilitates searches combining IPC symbols with applicant/inventor names, titles, abstracts and family information; it is used to manage reclassification and revision updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard expressions and terminology (glossary) for consistent interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of standard expressions is provided (e.g., 'Covered' or 'Provided for', expressions indicating residual or combination subject matter, 'i.e.', 'e.g.', 'A and B', 'A or B') along with a glossary of classification terms with contextual meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the glossary definitions and standard expressions to interpret titles, references, notes and scheme entries consistently. Definitions in the Classification override glossary explanations for the places concerned.
